title: Neurodivergence — Reading the Map Without the Legend
hook: An autistic colleague who never meets your eye may be listening harder than anyone in the room; your map of faces was drawn for a different country.
why:
Almost everything in this book so far has assumed a common body language: that people look at you when they listen, that a flat face means a flat mood, that stillness means attention and fidgeting means boredom. For most people, most of the time, those assumptions are close enough to be useful. For a sizeable minority they are simply wrong.

Neurodivergence is the umbrella term for brains that work differently from the majority, including autism, ADHD, dyslexia and related conditions. The World Health Organization estimates that about one child in a hundred is autistic, and many adults, particularly older men, were never diagnosed. ADHD is more common still. You almost certainly work with, live near or love someone whose body speaks a different dialect.

This chapter does not teach you to spot neurodivergence, which would be both unreliable and intrusive. It teaches you to notice when your readings are built on a map that does not fit, why first impressions of autistic people go wrong, why misunderstanding runs in both directions, how to re-read eye contact, movement and expression, and what to do instead of guessing.

teach.h: A different dialect, not a broken one.
teach.p:
Every reading in this book rests on a baseline, as Part I insisted: you learn what is normal for a person before you interpret a change. The trouble with neurodivergent people is not that they have no baseline. It is that their baseline differs from the one you carry around without noticing, the one built from thousands of interactions with people whose bodies behave much like yours.

An autistic man may look away while listening, speak in a level tone about something he cares about intensely, and stand very still or move in ways that soothe him. A man with ADHD may jiggle his leg, doodle or pace while thinking hard. Neither is sending the message a neurotypical reader would assume. The behaviour is the same; the meaning is not.

It helps to think of these as dialects. A dialect is not a broken version of a language. It is a complete system with its own rules, and speakers of different dialects misunderstand each other in predictable ways. Many autistic people now describe themselves this way, and the research reviewed in this chapter supports the idea that the problem lies between people rather than inside one of them.

Language matters here too. Many autistic people prefer to be called autistic rather than a person with autism, seeing it as part of who they are; others prefer the opposite. The safe course is to follow the person's own words. The figure here looks aside while someone speaks. In one person this is distraction. In another it is the way he listens best.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if neurodivergent people's behaviour carried the same meanings as everyone else's. The studies in this chapter show systematic differences in eye contact, movement and expression that do not mean what a neurotypical reader assumes.

teach.h: First impressions go wrong in seconds.
teach.p:
In 2017 Noah Sasson and his colleagues filmed autistic and non-autistic adults taking part in a mock audition and showed short clips, a few seconds long, to hundreds of observers. The observers rated the autistic adults less favourably on several counts. They were seen as more awkward and less likeable, and observers said they would be less willing to talk to them, live near them or sit next to them.

The most revealing part of the study was what happened when observers saw only a transcript of what each person said. The difference disappeared, and on some measures the autistic participants were rated more favourably. Their words were as good as anyone's. The negative impression came from how they looked and sounded while saying them: their gaze, their expressions, their movement and the music of their voices.

These judgments were made in seconds, without any information about diagnosis. The observers were not prejudiced against autism as such. They were doing what this book has described from the start, forming impressions from thin slices of behaviour, and applying a map that did not fit.

The practical lesson is that your first impression of someone who seems awkward, cold or odd is especially likely to be wrong if that person is neurodivergent. Before you decide, look at what they actually say and do. The figure here stands at rest, neither warm nor cold. A reader who sees coldness here is supplying it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if impressions of autistic adults were as negative from transcripts as from video. Sasson and colleagues found the negative impressions came from the clips, not from what the people said.

teach.p:
For decades, autism was described as a deficit in social understanding: autistic people were said to lack the ability to read other minds. In 2012 the autistic sociologist Damian Milton challenged this framing. He argued that when an autistic and a non-autistic person misunderstand each other, the failure runs both ways. The non-autistic person struggles to read the autistic person just as much, but only one of them is labelled as having a problem. He called this the double empathy problem.

In 2020 Catherine Crompton and her colleagues tested the idea. They asked people to pass a story along a chain, each person retelling it to the next, as in the children's game of telephone. Chains made up entirely of autistic people passed on the information about as accurately as chains made up entirely of non-autistic people. Mixed chains, alternating between the two, lost the most detail. Participants also reported less rapport in mixed pairs.

In other words, autistic people communicated effectively with each other. The breakdown happened at the boundary between dialects, not inside one of them. A later replication by the same group found the same pattern.

This changes the reader's job. If you find someone hard to read, that is information about the meeting of your two styles, not a verdict on them. It also means the effort of bridging the gap should be shared, not left to the person who is in the minority. The figures here stand at an angle, each reading the other. Both may be getting it wrong.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if autistic people communicated poorly with each other as well as with non-autistic people. Crompton and colleagues found autistic chains as accurate as non-autistic ones, with the losses concentrated in mixed chains.
teach.pullQuote: If you find someone hard to read, that is information about the meeting of your two styles, not a verdict on them.

teach.p:
No signal in this book is more often misread in neurodivergent people than eye contact. The chapter on gaze in Part I described research in which autistic adults reported that eye contact felt intense, uncomfortable or distracting, and that they looked away in order to concentrate on what was being said. Many describe sustained eye contact as overwhelming, like trying to listen to someone while a bright light shines in your face.

The usual readings of averted gaze are evasion, boredom, shyness or deceit. The chapter on deception in Part I explained why gaze aversion is a poor sign of lying in anyone. In autistic people it is often the opposite of disengagement: they are giving the conversation their full attention by removing a source of distraction.

Some autistic people have learned to fake eye contact, looking at the bridge of the nose or the mouth, or forcing themselves to hold a gaze while counting seconds. This can make them seem more conventional, but it costs effort and attention, and it often leaves them with less capacity for the conversation itself. The next chapter, on masking, looks at that cost.

For a reader, the change is simple. Stop treating eye contact as evidence of attention, honesty or respect, at least until you know the person. If you need to know whether someone has understood, ask, or look at what they do afterwards. Never insist that someone look at you. The figure here looks down and away. In a conversation with an autistic colleague, this may be the posture of someone who is following every word.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if autistic people who looked away were generally less attentive or less honest. Their own accounts, and research on gaze and concentration, suggest that looking away often helps them attend.

teach.p:
Neurotypical readers tend to read stillness as attention and movement as restlessness or boredom. For many neurodivergent people the relationship runs the other way.

Part II's chapter on self-soothing described stimming: repetitive movements such as rocking, hand-flapping, finger-tapping or fiddling with an object, which many autistic people use to regulate their arousal and focus. Autistic adults describe these movements as calming, as a way of expressing emotion, and sometimes as a source of joy. Suppressing them, often because others stare, can make it harder to cope.

For ADHD, there is experimental evidence that movement supports thinking. In 2015 Dustin Sarver, Mark Rapport, Michael Kofler and their colleagues measured how much children moved while doing tasks that taxed working memory. Children with ADHD who moved more tended to perform better, while children without ADHD tended to perform worse when they moved more. The authors suggested that, for children with ADHD, movement may help keep the brain alert enough to work.

The implication is clear. A colleague who jiggles a leg, clicks a pen, doodles or paces while you talk may be listening better because of it. Asking them to sit still may cost them the very attention you wanted. The figure here sits with one heel raised, the beginning of a bounce. In one person it is nerves. In another it is how concentration feels from the inside.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if movement always reduced attention. Sarver and colleagues found that, for children with ADHD, more movement went with better working memory performance, though the study involved children rather than adults.

teach.h: Faces and voices that do not follow the script.
teach.p:
Neurodivergent people may also express emotion differently in their faces and voices. In 2016 Rebecca Brewer, Geoffrey Bird and their colleagues asked autistic and non-autistic people to pose facial expressions of emotion, then asked observers to identify them. The expressions posed by autistic people were recognised less accurately, and, strikingly, autistic observers found them just as hard to read as non-autistic observers did.

The researchers concluded that autistic people's expressions were not following a shared autistic style but were individual. Each person's face had its own way of showing feeling. That fits what many autistic people say about themselves: that their face does not always show what they feel, or shows it in a way others misread.

Voices vary too. An autistic man may speak in a level tone about something he loves, or sound blunt when he means to be clear. A man with ADHD may interrupt because he fears losing a thought, not because he does not respect yours. Literal speech, missed hints and unusual timing are common.

The safest approach is to take words at face value and to read changes against the person's own baseline, not against a general template. A flat face is not a sign of a flat mood until you know that, in this person, it is. The figure here tilts his head slightly while listening. On one face this would read as interest. On another it might be the only sign of interest you will see.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if autistic people's facial expressions were as readable as anyone's. Brewer and colleagues found their posed expressions were recognised less accurately by autistic and non-autistic observers alike.

teach.p:
If your map does not fit, the answer is not a better map of autistic or ADHD body language. It is to stop relying on maps and start asking.

Ask rather than infer. If you are unsure whether someone is interested, upset or finished, ask plainly: Do you want to keep going with this, or stop here? Most neurodivergent people find direct questions a relief. State your own meaning rather than hinting. If something is urgent, say so; if you are joking, say so; if you are disappointed, say what about. Hints and tone that most people decode automatically may be missed.

Adjust the setting. Many people find it easier to talk side by side than face to face, as Part III described, or to talk while walking, or to follow up in writing. Offer an agenda before a meeting. Give time to think before an answer is needed. Avoid unexpected touch. Do not demand eye contact.

Above all, do not diagnose. Noticing that someone's style is unusual is useful; deciding that they are autistic, and treating them accordingly, is not your call and is often wrong. The aim is to read every person as an individual and to make it easier for people of every kind to be understood. The figures here stand side by side, looking the same way, the arrangement that makes many conversations easier for everyone.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if asking directly and stating meaning plainly made conversations with neurodivergent people no easier. Autistic people's own accounts, and the double empathy research, suggest that clarity and shared effort reduce misunderstanding.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, no gaze required
poseGallery.dontCaption: Insisting he look you in the eye
poseGallery.annotation: Eye contact is not evidence of attention. Arrangements that take gaze out of the conversation help many people listen better.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Deciding a flat face means he is not interested
poseGallery.annotation: A flat face is not a flat mood until you know this person. Ask, and take the answer at face value.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Telling a colleague to sit still
poseGallery.annotation: For some people, movement is how attention works. Asking them to stop may cost the focus you wanted.

caseStudy:
Liam, thirty-four, manages a small software team. When Ravi joined, Liam formed an impression within a week. Ravi rarely looked at anyone in meetings, answered questions in a few flat words, never laughed at the team's jokes and sometimes said things like That approach will not work, without softening it. Liam decided he was disengaged, possibly arrogant, and began to wonder whether the hire had been a mistake.

Then he read Ravi's first written design review. It was the most careful document anyone on the team had produced, and it caught two problems Liam had missed. He asked Ravi for a one-to-one, and, rather than giving feedback about his manner, asked how he preferred to work.

Ravi told him, a little warily, that he was autistic. He said he looked away in meetings because faces distracted him from what people were saying, that he found the jokes hard to follow when several people talked at once, and that he said things directly because he assumed people wanted to know. He asked whether he could get agendas in advance and give some of his input in writing.

Liam agreed. He started sending agendas the day before, asking for written comments, and saying plainly what he meant instead of hinting. He stopped reading Ravi's gaze as a verdict. Within a few months, Ravi was the person the team relied on for reviews, and Liam had noticed that two other team members liked the agendas just as much. He also noticed how quickly he had been ready to write someone off on the strength of a manner.
observe: Notice someone this week whose manner you find hard to read, and write down what they actually said, separately from how they said it.
Notice your own reading of eye contact: whether you take looking away as a sign of boredom, shyness or evasion.
Notice people who move while they think, such as pacing, doodling or tapping, and whether their contributions suffer for it.
Notice how often you hint rather than say what you mean, and whether anyone misses the hint.

drills.name: Words Without the Body
steps: Think of a colleague or acquaintance whose manner you find awkward or cold.
Write down three things they said recently, word for word if you can.
Read the words back as if from a stranger, without picturing their face or voice.
Note whether your impression of them changes.
Decide on one thing you will judge by their words and actions rather than their manner.

drills.name: Say It Plainly
steps: For one day, notice each time you hint instead of stating what you want or mean.
Rewrite three of those hints as plain statements.
Use one of the plain versions in a real conversation.
Note how the other person responded.

drills.name: Offer the Format
steps: Before your next meeting or important conversation, send a short agenda or the key question in writing.
Offer a choice of how to respond: in the meeting, by message afterwards, or in a walk-and-talk.
Notice who takes up which option.
Ask one person afterwards whether it helped.

drills.name: Gaze Audit
steps: In your next three conversations, notice how much eye contact you expect and how you react when it is missing.
Each time someone looks away, ask yourself what else might explain it.
Write down one occasion when you assumed something about gaze that turned out to be wrong.
Keep the note where you will see it.

quiz.q: A manager says that a team member who never meets his eye in meetings is probably not paying attention. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, because eye contact is the most reliable sign of attention in any person
For many autistic people, looking away is how they concentrate on what is being said
Averted gaze is a reliable sign of deceit, so the team member is likely hiding something
Gaze means nothing in anyone, so managers should never pay any attention to it at all
quiz.explain: Many autistic adults report that eye contact is intense or distracting and that they look away in order to listen. Gaze is a poor guide to attention or honesty until you know the person's baseline.

quiz.q: What did Sasson and colleagues find when observers judged autistic adults from transcripts alone?
options: The autistic adults were rated even more harshly than they had been from the video clips
The negative impressions disappeared, and on some measures autistic adults were rated more favourably
Observers could tell from the transcripts alone which speakers were autistic and which were not
Transcripts produced the same ratings as video, so the impressions came from the words
quiz.explain: The negative first impressions came from how the autistic adults looked and sounded in short clips, not from what they said. Their words were as well received as anyone's.

quiz.q: In Crompton and colleagues' study, which chains passed on a story least accurately?
options: Chains made up entirely of autistic people
Chains made up entirely of non-autistic people
Mixed chains, alternating autistic and non-autistic people
All the chains lost information at exactly the same rate
quiz.explain: Autistic chains were about as accurate as non-autistic ones. The losses were greatest in mixed chains, which fits Milton's idea that misunderstanding happens between dialects rather than inside one.

quiz.q: What does Milton's double empathy problem propose?
options: Autistic people have twice as much empathy as others, which overwhelms them
Non-autistic people should learn to imitate autistic body language exactly
Empathy can be measured twice, once from the face and once from the voice
Misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic people runs in both directions
quiz.explain: Milton argued that difficulties in communication arise between people with different ways of being, not from a deficit in one of them. Both sides struggle to read the other.

quiz.q: During a planning meeting, a colleague bounces his leg, doodles constantly and rarely looks up, yet his comments are sharp and relevant. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask him privately to sit still and look at the speaker, so he seems more engaged in meetings
Let him be, since for some people movement and looking away help them concentrate
Conclude that he is bored, and give his part of the project to someone more attentive
Raise his behaviour with the rest of the team, so that everyone can help him to change
quiz.explain: His contributions show he is attending. For some people, especially with ADHD or autism, movement and averted gaze support concentration, and suppressing them can cost the attention you want.

quiz.q: A new team member who has told you he is autistic gives short, blunt answers and seems uncomfortable in group discussion. What is the most useful step?
options: Ask how he prefers to communicate, and offer agendas and written options
Coach him to smile more and soften his answers, so others warm to him
Avoid involving him in discussions, so that he is not made uncomfortable
Explain to the team that he cannot read people, so that they make allowances
quiz.explain: Asking about preferences and offering formats that suit him shares the work of bridging the gap. Coaching him to perform a different style places the whole burden on him.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person whose manner you have found hard to read or have judged quickly: a colleague, a relative, someone at a club. Describe what you noticed about their eye contact, expression, voice or movement, and what you concluded. Now write down what they actually said and did, separate from how they came across. Could your reading have been built on a map that does not fit them? What one thing could you ask them, or change, to understand them better?
reflection.guidance: You do not need to know or guess whether the person is neurodivergent. The point is to notice where your impression rests on manner rather than substance, and to find a way to ask instead of infer. Be specific about the moment and about what you could do differently next time.

failureMode: The first failure is to read averted gaze as evasion, boredom or disrespect, when for many people it is how they listen. The second is to trust a first impression of someone who seems awkward or cold, when research shows such impressions are built on manner rather than substance. The third is to treat misunderstanding as the other person's deficit, when it runs in both directions. The fourth is to ask someone to sit still, look up or smile more, when their movement or stillness may be what lets them think. The fifth is to hint and expect to be understood. And the sixth is to diagnose: deciding someone is autistic or has ADHD, and treating them as a category rather than a person.

watch.notice: Autistic adults on first dates, speaking for themselves. Notice the range: some look away while listening, some speak in level tones about things they love, some say exactly what they think. Then notice how much warmth there is, once you stop reading it through the usual map.

watch.title: The world needs all kinds of minds
watch.notice: An autistic scientist speaking to a large audience. Notice her direct, unadorned delivery and her gaze, and how quickly the content takes over from the manner if you let it.
